DILG Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA corner Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City http: //www.dilg.com.ph DILG OPINION No. 84 s. 2022 SEP 06 2022 HON. BRIAN JAMES J. LU Chairman Quezon City Council for Sectoral Representatives Office of the Sanggunian, Quezon City Dear Hon. Lu: This pertains to your letter dated 9 August 2022 requesting for legal opinion on whether the Contract of Service (COS) and Job Order (JO) personnel of a Local Government Unit (LGU) may be elected as sectoral representatives to the sanggunian. The antecedent facts are follows• • The Quezon City Council of Sectoral Representatives (QCCSR) are on the process of accreditation of NGOs/Pos, organization and association in Quezon City for purposes of election of sectoral representatives. • During the orientation presided by the representative of the DILG-Bureau of Local Government Supervision, it was mentioned that to be able to be lected as representative of a particular sector, the representative of the NGOs/Pos, organization or associations should not be a government employees to avoid conflict of interest. Said representative stated that all persons who receive salary from the government such as Contract of Service, Job Orders and Consultants are considered government employee. The argument submitted is that Contract of Service (COS) and Job Order (JO) personnel as well as consultants are not government employees as defined by law as there is no employer-employee relationship in the nature of their services, hence, are qualified to be elected as sectoral representative. Hence, your request for legal opinion. We opine in the negative. Contract of Service (COS) and Job Order (JO) personnel are not qualified to be elected as sectoral representatives to the Sanggunian. We agree to the argument that there is no employer-employee relationship attached to the services Contract of Service (COS) and Job Order (JO) personnel. It is well "Matino, Mahusay at Maaasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

enunciated in the case of Lopez, et.al. vs. MWSSI citing CSC Memorandum Circular No. 38. The CSC, as well as the Court of Appeals, makes much of CSC Memorandum Circular No. 38, Series of 1993, which distinguishes between contract of servicesoob services and contractual appointment. The Circular provides: Contract of Services and Job Orders are different from Contractual appointment and Plantilla appointment of casual employees, respectively, which are required . to be submitted to CSC for approval. Contracts of Services and Job Orders refer to employment described as follows: I. The contract covers lump sum work or services such as janitorial, security or consultancy services where no employer-employee relationship exist; 2. The job order covers piece of work or intermittent job of short duration not exceeding six months on a daily basis; 3. The contract of services and job orders are not covered by Civil Service Law, Rules and Regulations; [sic] but covered by COA rules; 4. The employees involved in the contracts or job orders do not enjoy the benefits enjoined by government employees, such as PERA, COLA and RATA. 5. As the services rendered under contracts of services and job orders are not considered government services, they do not have to be submitted to the Civil Service Commission for approval. However, we submit that the non-existence of employer-employee relationship does not divest the existence of conflict of interest sought to be avoided in the case of sectoral representation in the Sanggunian. R.A. No. 6713, otherwise known as the "Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees" defined Conflict of Interest as follows: (i) "Conflict of interest" arises when a public official or employee is a member of a board, an officer, or a substantial stockholder of a private corporation or owner or has a substantial interest in a business, and the interest of such corporation or business, or his rights or duties therein, may be opposed to or affected by the faithful performance of official duty. On the other hand, the Legal Information Institute2 defined conflict of interest simply as one that refer to ethical problems that may arise between parties with a pre-existing relationship. The pre-existing relationship does not have to be an employer-employee relationship, it may be a contractual relationship such as that of a COS and JO. To elaborate further, while COS and JO personnel are not considered employees in the "technical sense" as they are not holders of plantilla positions in the civil service, the nature of their work however having no security of tenure puts them in a situation I G.R. No. 154472; 30 June 2005 https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/conflict of

where their contracts with the former are at the disposal of the public incumbent local officials. Ergo, they are susceptible to being used as channels to advance any beneficial-personal interests of some local officials to the agenda of the local legislative body. It is from this respect that the DILG field officer who attended the orientation probably applied the concept of conflict of interest in R.A. No. 6713 not in the "technical sense" but in "analogous manner". The COS and JO personnel are considered in an analogous situation with that of government employees insofar as avoidance of conflict of interest in sectoral representation is concerned because of the pre-existing contractual relationship of COS and JO personnel with the LGU concerned. In addition, allowing COS and JO personnel to be sectoral representatives in the sanggunian will be violative of the rule against double compensation. In DILG Opinion No. 62 s. 2018, the Department cited the Decision of the Ombudsman in "Field Investigation Office vs. Josephine H. Abalecio" docketed as OMB-V-A-17- 0123 in this wise: "We agree with the decision of the Ombudsman in the case entitled, "Field Investigation Office vs. Josephine H. Abelacio", docketed as OMB- V-A-17-0123 that although services rendered under Job Order contracts are not considered govemment services as there is no employer- employee relationship created between the govemment and the Job Order employee, the compensation received out of the contract is sourced from government funds also, thus, technically, receiving double compensation from the government which is proscribed under Section 8, Article IX (B) of the Constitution and Section 95 of the Local Government Code, to wit: "SECTION 8. No elective or appointive public officer or employee shall receive additional, double, or indirect compensation, unless specifically authorized by law, nor accept without the consent of the Congress, any present, emolument, office, or title of any kind from any foreign government. Pensions or gratuities shall not be considered as additional, double, or indirect compensation. " and "SECTION 94. Appointment of Elective and Appointive Local Officials; Candidates Who Lost in Election. - (a) No elective or appointive local official shall be eligible for appointment or designation in any capacity to any public office or position during his tenure. Unless otherwise allowed by law or by the primary functions of his position, no elective or appointive local official shall hold any other office or employment in the govemment or any subdivision, agency 45 or instrumentality controlled thereof, including government-owned or corporations or their subsidiaries. (b) Except for losing candidates in Barangay elections, no candidate who lost in any election shall, within one (I) year after such election, be appointed to any office in the govemment or any government- owned or -controlled corporations or in any of their subsidiaries. "

Moreover, to allow job orders and contracts of services as exemption would be to indirectly permit an act that is directly prohibited by the Constitution on double compensation. It would be an interpretation that collides with the spirit and the intention of the prohibition. What is directly prohibited cannot be indirectly permitted. If such interpretation and practice is tolerated, the prohibition can be so easily evaded, as if no qualified other persons were available, therefore qualifying for a job order • basis hiring. " This opinion is issued without prejudice to contrary ruling or opinion of competent courts and/or authorities on the matter. We hope to have addressed your concern accordingly. Thank you. Very truly yours, BY AUTHORITY OF THE SECRETARY: I AN Undersecr ry for Local Government OUSLG/MLWLLLS-LRALLD,'kbm/ClP copy furnished: DIRECTOR MARIA LOURDES L.
